headline: How to spot
a market bottom
subhead: Five signals that the selloff's core worries are fading

items.title: Bad news stops biting
items.body: Tariff shocks, weak jobs or guidance cuts hit at the open, then stocks recover or close higher — bad news stops working.

items.title: The leaders stop falling
items.body: Big Tech and semis led the drop and carry the most index weight. Watch AI capex worries ease and the chip index stop making new lows — not one stock's bounce.

items.title: Risk appetite returns
items.body: Money rotates from utilities and staples back toward growth. Earnings get judged on improvement, not just misses. More sectors stabilizing means confidence returning.

items.title: Credit spreads stay calm
items.body: Check the US high-yield spread (FRED: BAMLH0A0HYM2). New equity lows with a flat or falling spread mean corporate credit stress is not worsening.

items.title: A higher low forms
items.body: One-day surges can be short covering. Watch a rebound, then a pullback holding above the prior low — a higher low — then a break above the rebound high.

takeaway: No single signal calls the bottom. Bear rallies still happen — know your cash needs, then scale in or buy monthly.
caption:
What actually changes when a market bottoms?
Five quiet signals: bad news stops biting, semis stop making lows, credit holds.
None of them calls the exact low.
notes: OPM rebuild of a Chinese explainer on identifying market bottoms. All five angles, the FRED series code and the closing caveat are preserved; Chinese text translated to English.
